item.title: Two-Sided Plausibility Constraints in Persuasion
item.description: arXiv:2610.13702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A sender with commitment provides additional information to an already informed receiver. Final posterior means must be more dispersed than initial means and less dispersed than the state, in convex order. We characterize when these two plausibility constraints are also sufficient, so that every distribution satisfying them can be induced. If the state has a positive density, they are sufficient exactly under interval-partition information: the receiver learns which interval of a partition contains the state and nothing more, where an interval may be a single point. Otherwise, a nonempty open set of distributions satisfying both constraints cannot be induced, even when the sender observes the receiver's information. We use the sufficient case to derive an optimal symmetric disclosure rule in a second-price auction where bidders initially know valuation intervals.
item.dc:creator: Constantine Sorokin

item.title: Childcare Waitlists
item.description: arXiv:2610.12732v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Parents seeking childcare often face long waitlists. At the same time, vacancies at childcare centers can remain unfilled for extended periods. We trace this paradox to two persistent features of childcare services. First, families consider multiple child care options due to enrollment uncertainties, resulting in phantom listings that remain on waitlists even after families have found care elsewhere or no longer need a slot. Second, filling a slot is time-consuming: centers learn whether a family is actively seeking enrollment only after making an offer and waiting for a response. As families pursue alternatives while they wait and their children age, these delays and feedback effects amplify the mismatch between demand and available capacity. We study two operational remedies. First, we examine regular verification that removes phantom listings before offers are made, improving the efficiency of enrollment and reducing vacancies. Second, we study mixed-age classrooms, in which some slots designated for older children can be flexibly used by younger children. This flexibility increases utilization, shortens waits, and reduces wasted offers. Its benefits extend beyond conventional pooling: as children move between age groups, classrooms can be filled through internal flows rather than costly external search, further reducing enrollment delays. Together, verification and mixed use offer a way to expand effective capacity in early childhood classrooms, where regulatory and operational constraints make adding physical capacity particularly costly.
item.dc:creator: Yueyang Zhong, Jun Li, Senthil Veeraraghavan

item.title: The False Allure of "Security by Obscurity": A Game-Theoretic Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.12858v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: "Security by obscurity," or the idea that hiding how a system works helps protect it from adversaries, has long been poorly regarded in the security community. Yet its intuitive appeal persists, and it has resurfaced repeatedly in industry practices and public debates over the years. The logic, on the one hand, is that open scrutiny of systems is the best way to find and respond to problems; and on the other hand, that too much openness can increase risk by giving adversaries a roadmap for attack. This isn't purely a technical question, but a human one: it's about how attackers and good-faith security researchers respond to openness in the real world. As such, security experts base their stance on decades of community experience; however, the field lacks empirical or theoretical foundations to back up these long-standing beliefs. We provide the first rigorous modeling of "security by obscurity," aiming to capture how rational actors will respond to openness or obscurity in fallible systems. We prove that in equilibrium under realistic model conditions, "obscured" systems are more likely to suffer successful attacks than "open" systems --- establishing theoretical support for the longstanding received wisdom.
item.dc:creator: In-Uck Park, Sunoo Park

item.title: Dynamic Matching with Abandonment: Optimal Guarantees via Static Priority Policies
item.description: arXiv:2610.12991v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study stochastic dynamic matching with abandonment, a fundamental model in which agents of different types arrive over time, may abandon the market while waiting, and can be matched in pairs for rewards that depend on their types. No online policy can guarantee more than $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark, which knows all arrival and departure times. Whether this guarantee is achievable has been a central open problem, even in special cases. We resolve this problem by showing that, on every instance, a simple static priority policy, which is computable in polynomial time, earns at least $0.5$ of the omniscient benchmark. This establishes that the optimal competitive ratio is exactly $0.5$, improving the previous best guarantee of 0.192 for the general model [Li et al. 2026; Collina et al. 2020] Our analysis rests on a key stochastic result, which is a new lower bound on the probability that some agent from a given set of types is available. Building on this bound, we develop two approaches: a primal approach that reads the priorities from an optimal solution of a novel linear program, and a dual approach that assigns a ``value'' to each type, and prioritizes matches with high ``surplus'' (reward minus value of involved agents). These values are the unique solution of a fixed-point equation derived from linear programming duality. We also show that the two approaches are closely connected.
item.dc:creator: Nick Arnosti, Rad Niazadeh, Pranav Nuti, Felipe Simon

item.title: Convex Choice
item.description: arXiv:2406.19063v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For multidimensional Euclidean type spaces, we study convex choice: from any choice set, the set of types that make the same choice is convex. We establish that, in a suitable sense, this property characterizes the sufficiency of local incentive constraints. Convex choice is also of interest more broadly, e.g., in cheap-talk games. We tie convex choice to a notion of directional single-crossing differences (DSCD). For an expected-utility agent choosing among lotteries, DSCD implies that preferences are either one-dimensional or must take the affine form that has been tractable in multidimensional mechanism design.
item.dc:creator: Navin Kartik, Andreas Kleiner

item.title: Who and How? Adverse Selection and flexible Moral Hazard
item.description: arXiv:2506.12979v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We characterize incentive-compatible mechanisms in environments with hidden types and flexible hidden actions. Our approach introduces extended recommendation schedules that also prescribe actions off path, after misreports. This yields a tractable and complete characterization of incentive compatibility, which includes a generalized integral monotonicity condition capturing the interaction between adverse selection and moral hazard. We illustrate the usefulness of the characterization in a range of applications, including franchise agreements, employment contracts, and optimal taxation, covering both risk neutrality and risk aversion, with and without limited liability. Among other results, we identify a broad class of environments in which menus of affine contracts are optimal for a profit maximizing principal.
item.dc:creator: Henrique Castro-Pires, Deniz Kattwinkel, Jan Knoepfle

item.title: When Do Markets Work? Multiplex Networks and Efficiency
item.description: arXiv:2605.21117v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study an Arrow-Debreu economy with externalities generated by multiplex networks. Market equilibrium prices reflect not only preferences and the scarcity of goods, but also consumers' network positions induced by goods-specific externalities and the linkages across goods arising from the endogenous budget constraint. We quantify the departures of equilibrium allocations from Pareto efficiency using both a utility-based measure of efficiency loss and a coefficient of resource utilization, thereby linking network multiplexity quantitatively to equilibrium performance. These measures also identify zero-efficiency-loss cases: competitive equilibria are efficient when the relevant network-centrality vectors are parallel, a condition satisfied, in particular, when all networks are regular or when all layers share the same network structure. When competitive markets allocate goods inefficiently, a Lindahl equilibrium implemented through personalized prices can restore efficiency, although it may leave some consumers worse off.
item.dc:creator: Chengqing Li, Yves Zenou, Junjie Zhou

item.title: Endogenous shareholding auctions
item.description: arXiv:2607.02457v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We introduce endogenous shareholding auctions for production economies where a designer must elicit demand in order to determine price and quantity. Each of these auctions has the property that the auction's profit is distributed across the designer and the bidders in accordance with ownership shares that are determined over the course of the auction. We characterize this class, and a larger class, on the basis of standard axioms. Finally, we investigate optimal auctions according to both prior-free domination and subjective expected welfare. Applications include public housing, voluntary separation, and monopoly regulation.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Mackenzie, Christian Trudeau

item.title: Optimal growth under irreversible pollution: The Forster-Ramsey model
item.description: arXiv:2609.12693v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study optimal growth in a Ramsey economy with irreversible pollution, where the natural absorption capacity is non-monotonic and non-concave a la Forster. In the absence of pollution control, the capital dynamics decouple from pollution, and we characterize a simple threshold on the maximal absorption capacity above which the optimal path is sustainable and below which an optimal regime of irreversible pollution sets in. We then introduce an optimal abatement pollution control to assess whether irreversible pollution ceases to be optimal. We derive a four-dimensional dynamical system for capital, consumption, pollution and the (shadow) cost of pollution, coupled with an algebraic rule for optimal abatement. First, we show that while optimal abatement does shift the irreversibility threshold, it may not rule out optimal irreversible pollution paths. Second, and more importantly, we show that embedding the Forster's pollution dynamics into a Ramsey growth model generates a novel and robust hybrid ecological-economic irreversibility condition that is invisible in pollution-only frameworks. Coupling ecosystem curvature with the social discount rate, it is structurally robust and preeminent over all feasibility conditions amenable to policy intervention, and defines the boundary between a world where sustainability is achievable and one where it is not.
item.dc:creator: Raouf Boucekkine, Natalia Hritonenko, Yuri Yatsenko, Ullrika Sahlin

item.title: The Robustness of Sequential Implementation under Information Perturbations
item.description: arXiv:2609.30464v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Bayesian monotonicity is a necessary condition for full implementation in Bayes-Nash equilibrium. Under the sequential equilibrium refinement, however, multi-stage mechanisms can expand the scope for implementation. We show that this additional implementation power is fragile. Whenever a multi-stage mechanism sequentially implements a social choice correspondence that is not Bayesian monotone, we construct arbitrarily small "information perturbations" and show that there are sequential equilibria under these perturbations that yield inadmissible decisions with probability bounded away from zero. Under these perturbations, players' types are not independent conditional on the state and some player is sometimes uncertain of their payoff type. We show by example that the general result fails if perturbations are required to satisfy conditional independence or "known payoff types."
item.dc:creator: Ian Ball, Drew Fudenberg, Stephen Morris

item.title: Endogenous Information Design and Informational Evolution in Dynamic Economic Systems with Incentives and Learning
item.description: arXiv:2609.36093v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: This paper studies the endogenous informational evolution of dynamic economic systems. Building on Hurwicz's conceptual framework, such a system is defined as a dynamic joint adjustment process of resource and information allocation linked by recursive feedback. Economic theory gains precision by isolating particular margins, but when information production, disclosure, learning, incentives, actions, and future feasibility interact across these two processes, conclusions obtained by holding other margins fixed need not survive their joint determination. The paper develops a system-level dynamic equilibrium framework for this interaction. Holding particular links fixed yields familiar environments in dynamic mechanism design, information design, experimentation and learning, feedback and disclosure, and information acquisition. The analysis establishes three central failures relative to fixed or partially exogenous informational environments: informational efficiency under exogenous feasibility is generally incompatible with endogenous dynamic feasibility; incentive and disclosure design cannot generally be separated; and informational monotonicity can fail without implementation replicability. It also identifies the corresponding positive boundaries. Optimal disclosure may be interior or extreme; bang--bang disclosure arises under additional conditions, and a further specialization generates an endogenous transition from opacity to transparency. Information may therefore be optimally withheld even when its direct decision value is strictly positive. Extensions to private payoff-relevant information and limited commitment preserve the recursive structure.
item.dc:creator: Guoqiang Tian

item.title: Submission quotas as self-screening when manuscript production is cheap
item.description: arXiv:2610.04688v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Generative AI enables authors to produce more manuscripts at lower cost. But evaluation by expert editors and referees remains scarce. In this context, the value of an author's submission rights can increase. Major research repositories and journals are reacting by imposing submission quotas and fees. Non-transferable author quotas transform submission of a manuscript into a revealed-priority decision. Authors construct a portfolio of their highest-ranked manuscripts. A common fee charges an author for every manuscript they submit. Both methods have drawbacks. Quotas do not flexibly allocate scarce review capacity to authors who have unusually strong realised candidate sets. Fees can generate heterogeneous submission thresholds that may be systematically related to an author's baseline portfolio quality. In this paper, I derive the condition under which submission quotas yield weakly higher mean reviewed value than fees, given an equal expected review load. When project values are bounded and candidate manuscripts are abundant, an equal-load fee can price out some authors entirely.
item.dc:creator: Steve Lawford

item.title: Smart Lotteries in School Choice: Ex-ante Pareto-Improvement with Ex-post Stability
item.description: arXiv:2602.10679v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In school choice, students typically have strict preferences over the schools while the schools have coarse priorities over the students based on their distance and their enrolled siblings. The outcome of a centralized admission mechanism is then usually obtained by the Deferred Acceptance (DA) algorithm with random tie-breaking. Therefore, every outcome of this mechanism that occurs with a positive probability is a stable solution for the coarse priorities. This implies a probabilistic assignment, specifying the admission probability for each student-school pair. In this paper, we propose a new efficiency-improving stable 'smart lottery' mechanism. We aim to improve the probabilistic assignment ex-ante in a stochastic dominance sense, while ensuring that the improved random matching is still ex-post stable, meaning that it can be decomposed into stable matchings regarding the original coarse priorities. Therefore, this smart lottery mechanism can provide a clear Pareto-improvement in expectation for any cardinal utilities compared to the standard DA with lottery solution, without sacrificing the stability of the final outcome. We show that although the underlying computational problem is NP-hard, we can solve the problem in practice by using column generation. Our computational results show that the welfare gains by our mechanism are substantially larger than the expected gains by standard methods that realize efficiency improvements after ties have already been broken. Additionally, we illustrate for real-world school choice data of Ghent (Belgium) that, while not theoretically guaranteed, our mechanism can Pareto-improve upon methods that improve upon DA but violate ex-post stability, such as Efficiency-Adjusted Deferred Acceptance.
item.dc:creator: Haris Aziz, P\'eter Bir\'o, Gergely Cs\'aji, Tom Demeulemeester

item.title: Truthful Production Uncertainty in Electricity Markets: A Two-Stage Mechanism
item.description: arXiv:2604.02455v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Renewable power sources have low production costs, but may result in high balancing costs due to the inherent production uncertainty. Current day-ahead markets elicit only point production profiles and neglect the degree of uncertainty associated with each generating asset, preventing the market operator from accounting for balancing costs in day-ahead dispatch and ancillary service procurement. This increases the total system cost and undermines market efficiency, especially in renewable-heavy power systems. To address this, we propose a new market clearing paradigm based on a two-stage mechanism, where producers report their production forecast distribution in the day-ahead stage, followed by the realized production in the real-time stage. By extending the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) payments to the two-stage setting, we show appealing properties in terms of incentive compatibility and individual rationality. An electricity market case study validates the theoretical claims, illustrating the effectiveness of the proposed mechanism in reducing system cost.
item.dc:creator: Shobhit Singhal, Lesia Mitridati, Licio Romao
